reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: Typically autosomal dominant, with progressive loss of subcutaneous fat from the limbs and buttocks emerging around puberty
The Dunnigan (FPLD2) variety arises from LMNA (lamin A/C) mutations, while PPARG mutations cause FPLD3; other genes account for rarer forms
Fat is redistributed rather than absent, so patients often show facial, neck, and truncal sparing or accumulation giving a cushingoid or muscular limb appearance
Loss of peripheral fat storage capacity produces insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatic steatosis, acanthosis nigricans, and often early type 2 diabetes
Women are frequently recognised more readily than men because muscular, fat-depleted limbs are more conspicuous, and they have high rates of polycystic-ovary-type features
Leptin is usually near-normal or only modestly reduced, so leptin (metreleptin) replacement benefits mainly the more leptin-deficient or severely affected patients
Management centres on insulin sensitisers, aggressive triglyceride and glucose control, and screening for cardiac and hepatic complications
Diagnosis rests on the partial fat-distribution pattern, metabolic profile, family history, and confirmatory genetics
reference.pathophysiology: Familial partial lipodystrophy is a dominantly inherited disorder in which subcutaneous adipose tissue in the extremities and gluteal region is progressively lost, most often from mutations in LMNA (lamin A/C, FPLD2) that disrupt the nuclear lamina and adipocyte survival, or in PPARG (FPLD3) that impair adipocyte differentiation. Because the limbs lose their fat-storage capacity while other depots may be spared or expanded, ingested lipid overflows into liver and muscle, generating severe insulin resistance. This produces hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatic steatosis, acanthosis nigricans, and a strong predisposition to insulin-resistant diabetes and, in LMNA disease, associated myopathic and cardiac features.
additionalDifferentials: Cushing syndrome (owing to truncal fat and facial fullness)
Metabolic syndrome or ordinary type 2 diabetes with central adiposity
Multiple symmetric lipomatosis where truncal fat accumulates
additionalInvestigations: Regional fat quantification by DEXA or MRI to demonstrate limb fat loss with truncal sparing
Fasting lipids (triglycerides), glucose/HbA1c, and fasting insulin/C-peptide
Serum leptin to gauge suitability for leptin (metreleptin) replacement
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging for steatosis
Genetic testing of LMNA and PPARG and other FPLD-associated genes
redFlags: Conduction disease, arrhythmia, or cardiomyopathy in LMNA mutation carriers
Progressive fatty liver disease toward fibrosis
Rapidly deteriorating glycaemic control despite treatment
reference.prognosis: Long-term outlook is governed by metabolic and cardiovascular complications; with proactive control of triglycerides and diabetes and cardiac surveillance in laminopathy many patients do well, though premature cardiovascular disease and pancreatitis remain important risks.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the truncal fat and rounded face as Cushing syndrome
Overlooking limb fat loss in muscular-looking patients, especially men
Assuming leptin replacement will help all cases when leptin is often near-normal
Neglecting cardiac screening in LMNA-related disease
Ascribing the diabetes simply to lifestyle and missing the genetic cause
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on lipodystrophy
management: Manage insulin-resistant diabetes aggressively with metformin and insulin-sensitising therapy, escalating to high-dose insulin as required
Control hypertriglyceridaemia with fibrates and omega-3 fatty acids alongside dietary fat restriction to prevent pancreatitis
Offer leptin replacement (metreleptin) for patients with leptin deficiency and severe metabolic disease
Establish a foundation of a fat-controlled diet and regular exercise to limit ectopic lipid deposition and hepatic steatosis
Monitor and manage hepatic steatosis with liver function tests and imaging
Undertake cardiac surveillance in LMNA-related laminopathy for cardiomyopathy and conduction disease, with device therapy such as a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator where indicated
Provide genetic testing of LMNA and PPARG with counselling and family screening
